claim: The organotypic pancreatic slice preserves intact β-cell structure compared to isolated islets.
source: We demonstrate that the organotypic pancreatic slice, when compared with isolated islets, preserves intact β-cell structure, and enhances glucose-dependent Ca2+ responses and insulin secretion.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data showing preservation of ECM, capillaries, and β-cell polarity in slices versus isolated islets (Figure 1).

claim: The organotypic pancreatic slice enhances glucose-dependent Ca2+ responses compared to isolated islets.
source: We demonstrate that the organotypic pancreatic slice, when compared with isolated islets, preserves intact β-cell structure, and enhances glucose-dependent Ca2+ responses and insulin secretion.
evidence: Supported by Ca2+ imaging data showing faster responses and Ca2+ spikes at low glucose in slices (Figures 4-6).

claim: The organotypic pancreatic slice enhances insulin secretion compared to isolated islets.
source: We demonstrate that the organotypic pancreatic slice, when compared with isolated islets, preserves intact β-cell structure, and enhances glucose-dependent Ca2+ responses and insulin secretion.
evidence: Supported by insulin secretion assays showing higher secretion at all glucose concentrations in slices (Figure 3A).

claim: Integrins and FAK are exclusively activated at the β-cell capillary interface.
source: Integrins and FAK are exclusively activated at the β-cell capillary interface and using in situ and in vitro models we show their activation both positions presynaptic scaffold proteins, like ELKS and liprin, and regulates glucose-dependent Ca2+ responses and insulin secretion.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining showing integrin-β1 and phospho-FAK enrichment at capillary interface (Figure 1E, F).

claim: Integrin and FAK activation positions presynaptic scaffold proteins ELKS and liprin.
source: Integrins and FAK are exclusively activated at the β-cell capillary interface and using in situ and in vitro models we show their activation both positions presynaptic scaffold proteins, like ELKS and liprin, and regulates glucose-dependent Ca2+ responses and insulin secretion.
evidence: Supported by data showing disruption of ELKS and liprin positioning after FAK inhibition or integrin blockade (Figures 8-9).

claim: Integrin and FAK activation regulates glucose-dependent Ca2+ responses.
source: Integrins and FAK are exclusively activated at the β-cell capillary interface and using in situ and in vitro models we show their activation both positions presynaptic scaffold proteins, like ELKS and liprin, and regulates glucose-dependent Ca2+ responses and insulin secretion.
evidence: Supported by data showing reduced Ca2+ responses after FAK inhibition with Y15 (Figure 7C, D) and integrin-β1 blockade (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).

claim: Integrin and FAK activation regulates glucose-dependent insulin secretion.
source: Integrins and FAK are exclusively activated at the β-cell capillary interface and using in situ and in vitro models we show their activation both positions presynaptic scaffold proteins, like ELKS and liprin, and regulates glucose-dependent Ca2+ responses and insulin secretion.
evidence: Supported by data showing reduced insulin secretion after FAK inhibition with Y15 (Figure 7E, Figure 9D).

claim: FAK orchestrates the final steps of glucose-dependent insulin secretion within the restricted domain where β-cells contact the islet capillaries.
source: We conclude that FAK orchestrates the final steps of glucose-dependent insulin secretion within the restricted domain where β-cell contact the islet capillaries.
evidence: Supported by data showing FAK activation at capillary interface, its role in positioning scaffold proteins, and regulating Ca2+ responses and secretion.

claim: The region where β-cells contact the islet capillaries is specialized for secretion.
source: Accumulating evidence suggests that the region where β-cell contact the islet capillaries is specialised for secretion (Gan et al., 2017; Low et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work and data in this manuscript showing targeted granule fusion (Figure 2).

claim: β cells within intact islets make a discrete point of contact with the extracellular matrix that surrounds the capillaries.
source: β cells, within intact islets, make a discrete point of contact with the extracellular matrix (ECM) that surrounds the capillaries.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data showing laminin enrichment at capillaries in slices (Figure 1B).

claim: The point of contact between β cells and capillary ECM is the target for insulin granule fusion.
source: This point of contact is the target for insulin granule fusion (Low et al., 2014) and is enriched in presynaptic scaffold proteins, like liprin and ELKS and therefore has characteristics analogous to a neuronal presynaptic domain (Deng and Thorn, 2022; Lammert and Thorn, 2020; Low et al., 2014; Ohara-Imaizumi et al., 2019; Ohara-Imaizumi et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and granule fusion assay data (Figure 2).

claim: The capillary interface of β cells is enriched in presynaptic scaffold proteins like liprin and ELKS.
source: This point of contact is the target for insulin granule fusion (Low et al., 2014) and is enriched in presynaptic scaffold proteins, like liprin and ELKS and therefore has characteristics analogous to a neuronal presynaptic domain (Deng and Thorn, 2022; Lammert and Thorn, 2020; Low et al., 2014; Ohara-Imaizumi et al., 2019; Ohara-Imaizumi et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations and immunostaining data showing liprin enrichment at capillary interface (Figure 1G-J).

claim: The capillary interface of β cells has characteristics analogous to a neuronal presynaptic domain.
source: This point of contact is the target for insulin granule fusion (Low et al., 2014) and is enriched in presynaptic scaffold proteins, like liprin and ELKS and therefore has characteristics analogous to a neuronal presynaptic domain (Deng and Thorn, 2022; Lammert and Thorn, 2020; Low et al., 2014; Ohara-Imaizumi et al., 2019; Ohara-Imaizumi et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations and data showing enrichment of presynaptic scaffold proteins and targeted granule fusion.

claim: Local activation of integrins is the target for insulin granule fusion.
source: Recapitulating this domain by culture of β cells on ECM-coated dishes shows that local activation of integrins is the target for insulin granule fusion (Gan et al., 2018) and local control of microtubules regulates these secretory hot spots (Trogden et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and data showing targeted fusion at capillary interface where integrins are activated (Figures 1, 2).

claim: Ca2+ is the dominant regulator of insulin secretion principally by Ca2+ entry through voltage-sensitive Ca2+ channels.
source: Just like neurotransmitter release, Ca2+ is the dominant regulator of insulin secretion principally by Ca2+ entry through voltage-sensitive Ca2+ channels (Schulla et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: The location of Ca2+ channels relative to sites of granule fusion is critical to stimulus secretion coupling.
source: We know from other systems that the location of Ca2+ channels relative to sites of granule fusion is critical to stimulus secretion coupling (Nanou and Catterall, 2018; Stanley, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature from other systems.

claim: Ca2+ channels are typically regulated by intracellular Ca2+ concentrations leading to positive and negative feedback to control channel opening.
source: Ca2+ channels are typically regulated by intracellular Ca2+ concentrations leading to positive and negative feedback to control channel opening (Zühlke et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: In neurones, a presynaptic scaffold protein complex tethers synaptic vesicles and collocates Ca2+ channels to the presynaptic domain.
source: In neurones, a presynaptic scaffold protein complex tethers synaptic vesicles and collocates Ca2+ channels to the presynaptic domain (Südhof, 2012); whether similar mechanisms exist at the capillary interface of β cells is unknown.
evidence: Supported by citation to established neuroscience literature.

claim: There is functional evidence for close association of Cav1.2 Ca2+ channels and insulin granule exocytosis in β cells.
source: In β cells there is functional, in vitro, evidence for close association of Cav1.2, Ca2+ channels and insulin granule exocytosis (Bokvist et al., 1995; Gandasi et al., 2017; Pertusa et al., 1999) and structural evidence for protein links between the Cav1.2 channels and syntaxin 1A (Wiser et al., 1999); a SNARE protein required for granule fusion.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claim: There is structural evidence for protein links between Cav1.2 channels and syntaxin 1A in β cells.
source: In β cells there is functional, in vitro, evidence for close association of Cav1.2, Ca2+ channels and insulin granule exocytosis (Bokvist et al., 1995; Gandasi et al., 2017; Pertusa et al., 1999) and structural evidence for protein links between the Cav1.2 channels and syntaxin 1A (Wiser et al., 1999); a SNARE protein required for granule fusion.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous structural study.

claim: Syntaxin 1A has an even distribution across the β-cell plasma membrane with no enrichment at the capillary interface.
source: Immunostaining β cells in the more intact environment of pancreatic slices shows that syntaxin 1A (Low et al., 2014) has an even distribution across the β-cell plasma membrane and no enrichment at the capillary interface.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous immunostaining study.

claim: The scaffold protein ELKS interacts with the β subunit of the Ca2+ channel.
source: Instead, there is recent evidence that the scaffold protein ELKS interacts with the β subunit of the Ca2+ channel (Ohara-Imaizumi et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent study.

claim: The coupling between ELKS and the β subunit of Ca2+ channels enhances the Ca2+ response at residual capillary structures.
source: Furthermore, although the work was carried out in isolated islets, which lack capillaries, there was evidence that the coupling between ELKS and the β subunit enhanced the Ca2+ response at residual capillary structures (Ohara-Imaizumi et al., 2019), consistent with the idea that localised synaptic-like regulation of Ca2+ and exocytosis might exist in β cells (Deng and Thorn, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The pancreatic slice maintains complex cell-to-cell arrangements that are important for overall islet control such as an intact islet capillary bed.
source: Analogous to organotypic brain slices, pancreatic slices maintain complex cell-to-cell arrangements that are likely to be important for overall islet control such as an intact islet capillary bed (Cohrs et al., 2017; Gan et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies and immunostaining data (Figure 1).

claim: The local microenvironment around each endocrine cell is maintained in pancreatic slices, with each cell contacting the capillary and other endocrine cells.
source: In addition, the local microenvironment around each endocrine cell is maintained, with each cell contacting the capillary and other endocrine cells.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data showing preserved capillary contacts and cell-cell junctions (Figure 1).

claim: Pancreatic slices promote a distinct subcellular polarisation in β cells that is likely to impact on cell function.
source: This promotes a distinct subcellular polarisation in β cells that is likely to impact on cell function (Gan et al., 2017) with recent evidence the same organisation is present in rodent and human islets (Cottle et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations and immunostaining data showing polarized distribution of proteins (Figure 1).

claim: The same β-cell organization observed in slices is present in rodent and human islets.
source: This promotes a distinct subcellular polarisation in β cells that is likely to impact on cell function (Gan et al., 2017) with recent evidence the same organisation is present in rodent and human islets (Cottle et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent study.

claim: In isolated islets, laminin is not associated with any specific structure but is dotted throughout the islets.
source: In the isolated islets laminin was not associated with any specific structure but instead was dotted throughout the islets (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images showing dispersed laminin staining in isolated islets.

claim: In pancreatic slices, ECM identified by laminin is strongly enriched around the islet capillaries and in the islet capsule.
source: In pancreatic slices the ECM, identified by laminin, was strongly enriched around the islet capillaries and in the islet capsule (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images showing laminin enrichment at capillaries in slices.

claim: There is a reduction in laminin area in isolated islets compared to slices.
source: Consistent with this disruption we observed a reduction in laminin area and a reduction in CD31 (endothelial cell marker) immunostaining (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by quantification of immunofluorescence showing reduced laminin in isolated islets.

claim: There is a reduction in CD31 immunostaining in isolated islets compared to slices.
source: Consistent with this disruption we observed a reduction in laminin area and a reduction in CD31 (endothelial cell marker) immunostaining (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by quantification of immunofluorescence showing reduced CD31 in isolated islets.

claim: Phospho-FAK immunostaining shows significantly reduced area in β cells in isolated islets compared to slices.
source: Phospho-FAK immunostaining shows significantly reduced area (compared to total cell area, insulin + DAPI) in β cells in isolated islets (n = 29 cells in slices 112 cells in islets, Student's t-test p < 0.01).
evidence: Supported by quantification of phospho-FAK immunostaining area.

claim: In slices, integrin-β1 shows tight alignment with laminin-stained capillaries.
source: In slices, we observed tight alignment of integrin-β1 with laminin-stained capillaries (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images showing colocalization of integrin-β1 and laminin.

claim: Phosphorylated FAK is enriched at the capillary interface in slices.
source: Phosphorylated FAK (phospho-FAK) which provides a read out of focal adhesion activity (Rondas et al., 2012) was also enriched at the capillary interface (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images showing phospho-FAK enrichment at capillaries.

claim: In pancreatic slices, liprin shows enrichment at the capillary interface and very little staining in other regions around the β cell.
source: Using immunostaining in pancreatic slices, as expected, liprin showed enrichment at the capillary interface (stained with laminin) and very little staining in other regions around the β cell (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images and quantification showing liprin enrichment at capillary interface.

claim: In slices, the region adjacent to the capillary has significantly higher staining for both laminin and liprin.
source: In slices, the region adjacent to the capillary had significantly higher staining for both laminin and liprin (Figure 1H, I) as illustrated in a heatmap (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by quantification of fluorescence intensity in different regions around β cells.

claim: In isolated islets, integrin-β1 is misdistributed but still present all around the cells.
source: In isolated islets, consistent with the relative loss of ECM proteins (Figure 1A) we observed a misdistribution of integrin-β1 (Figure 1K), although interestingly, integrin-β1 was still present but was now all around the cells.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images showing dispersed integrin-β1 in isolated islets.

claim: In isolated islets, phospho-FAK is enriched at the residual capillaries.
source: Phospho-FAK was enriched at the residual capillaries (Figure 1L) but, using an area analysis, we observe a significant and approximately fivefold decrease in area occupied by phospho-FAK in the islets compared to slices (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images and quantification.

claim: There is an approximately fivefold decrease in area occupied by phospho-FAK in isolated islets compared to slices.
source: Phospho-FAK was enriched at the residual capillaries (Figure 1L) but, using an area analysis, we observe a significant and approximately fivefold decrease in area occupied by phospho-FAK in the islets compared to slices (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by quantification of phospho-FAK area.

claim: In isolated islets, liprin is dispersed and located all around the β-cell surface.
source: Also disrupted was the positioning of liprin. In isolated islets, liprin was dispersed and located all around the β-cell surface (Figure 1M).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images showing dispersed liprin in isolated islets.

claim: In isolated islets, liprin staining is evenly spread across all regions of the β-cell surface.
source: This alignment resulted in a significantly greater proportion of laminin staining in region 1 (Figure 1N) but the liprin staining was still evenly spread across all regions (Figure 1O) and illustrated in a heatmap (Figure 1P).
evidence: Supported by quantification of liprin fluorescence intensity across different regions.

claim: Lateral β-cell contacts are maintained in isolated islets, as shown by E-cadherin immunostaining.
source: We also show that β-cell structure is affected, lateral β-cell contacts were still maintained, as shown by E-cadherin immunostaining but Par3, normally located in the apical region of β cells, away from the capillaries showed diffuse non-polar organisation in isolated islets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images showing E-cadherin at cell-cell junctions.

claim: Par3 shows diffuse non-polar organisation in isolated islets.
source: We also show that β-cell structure is affected, lateral β-cell contacts were still maintained, as shown by E-cadherin immunostaining but Par3, normally located in the apical region of β cells, away from the capillaries showed diffuse non-polar organisation in isolated islets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images showing dispersed Par3 in isolated islets.

claim: In pancreatic slices, nearly 80% of all granule fusion events occur at the capillary interface.
source: Here, we repeat those findings and record each fusion event over a 20-min stimulus with high glucose (Figure 2A) but now, in parallel experiments, we compare the distribution of events obtained using pancreatic slices (Figure 2B). In both preparations targeting to the capillary interface of β cells is observed but in the slice preparation the targeting is significantly enhanced to the extent that nearly 80% of all granule fusion events occur in this region (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: Supported by quantification of granule fusion events using dye-tracing technique.

claim: The greater precision in targeting of insulin granule fusion in slices is consistent with the tight focus of phospho-FAK enrichment.
source: The greater precision in targeting of insulin granule fusion is consistent with the tight focus of phospho-FAK enrichment in slices (Figure 1F) and with previous in vitro reports that integrin activation drives granule targeting of granule fusion (Gan et al., 2018).
evidence: Inference based on correlation between phospho-FAK enrichment and granule fusion targeting, supported by citation.

claim: Pancreatic slices have significantly increased insulin secretion at all concentrations of glucose compared to isolated islets.
source: Here, we demonstrate that pancreatic slices, compared to isolated islets have, significantly increased insulin secretion at all concentrations of glucose (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by insulin secretion assay data showing dose-response curves.

claim: Pancreatic slices show insulin secretion at low glucose (2.8–5 mM) concentrations that is not seen in isolated islets.
source: Furthermore, we observed insulin secretion at low glucose (2.8–5 mM) concentrations in slices that was not seen in isolated islets, and the overall EC50 for glucose dose dependence was different (Figure 3A, EC50 10.2 mM for islets and 8.6 mM for slices).
evidence: Supported by insulin secretion assay data showing responses at low glucose in slices.

claim: The EC50 for glucose-dependent insulin secretion is 10.2 mM for isolated islets and 8.6 mM for slices.
source: Furthermore, we observed insulin secretion at low glucose (2.8–5 mM) concentrations in slices that was not seen in isolated islets, and the overall EC50 for glucose dose dependence was different (Figure 3A, EC50 10.2 mM for islets and 8.6 mM for slices).
evidence: Supported by fitted dose-response curves from insulin secretion data.

claim: Embedding isolated islets in agarose has no effect on insulin secretion.
source: In control experiments, embedding isolated islets in agarose (the substrate used to embed slices) had no effect in insulin secretion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by control experiment data comparing islets with and without agarose embedding.

claim: There is no difference in measured proinsulin secretion in slices compared to isolated islets.
source: Furthermore, there was no difference in measured proinsulin secretion in slices compared to isolated islets, indicating that insulin processing was unchanged (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by proinsulin secretion assay data.

claim: Glucose-dependent amplification is significantly larger in isolated islets compared with pancreatic slices.
source: In our experiments, because glucose-dependent secretion was greater in pancreatic slices at all glucose concentrations (Figure 3A), we were anticipating that amplification would be larger. Surprisingly, our results showed the opposite and in fact glucose-dependent amplification was significantly larger in isolated islets compared with pancreatic slices (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by insulin secretion measurements in the presence of diazoxide and high potassium.

claim: The overall decrease in glucose-dependent secretion in isolated islets compared to slices is due to reduced glucose-dependent triggering.
source: This enhanced amplification suggests the overall decrease in glucose-dependent secretion in isolated islets compared to slices (Figure 3A), must be due to reduced glucose-dependent triggering.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of amplification and total secretion data.

claim: Pretreatment with glibenclamide significantly increases insulin secretion measured at 2.8 mM glucose in both isolated islets and slices.
source: Pretreatment with the KATP channel blocker, glibenclamide (2 µM) significantly increased insulin secretion measured at 2.8 mM glucose in both isolated islets and slices (Student's t-test p < 0.01, n = 3 mice for both conditions).
evidence: Supported by insulin secretion assay data with glibenclamide treatment.

claim: Pretreatment with glibenclamide increases insulin secretion measured at 8 mM glucose only in isolated islets but not in slices.
source: In contrast, pretreatment with glibenclamide only increased insulin secretion measured at 8 mM in islets but not in slices (Student's t-test p < 0.05 for islets, p = 0.36 for slices, n = 3 mice for both conditions).
evidence: Supported by insulin secretion assay data with glibenclamide treatment at 8 mM glucose.

claim: β cells within slices typically show pulsatile Ca2+ activity even at 2.8 mM glucose.
source: In these recordings the Ca2+ responses from β cells within slices typically showed pulsatile activity even at 2.8 mM glucose (Figure 4D), which is consistent with the observations of insulin secretion at this low glucose concentration (Figure 3A), and we also observed rapid pulsing of Ca2+ at the beginning of the high glucose-induced responses in slices, consistent with enhanced excitability.
evidence: Supported by GCaMP6 Ca2+ imaging data showing pulsatile activity at low glucose.

claim: Rapid pulsing of Ca2+ at the beginning of high glucose-induced responses in slices is consistent with enhanced excitability.
source: In these recordings the Ca2+ responses from β cells within slices typically showed pulsatile activity even at 2.8 mM glucose (Figure 4D), which is consistent with the observations of insulin secretion at this low glucose concentration (Figure 3A), and we also observed rapid pulsing of Ca2+ at the beginning of the high glucose-induced responses in slices, consistent with enhanced excitability.
evidence: Inference based on observed rapid Ca2+ pulsing patterns.

claim: Ca2+ responses in slices are initiated almost simultaneously with the addition of 16.7 mM glucose.
source: Ca2+ responses in slices (Figure 5A, B) were apparently initiated almost simultaneously with the addition of 16.7 mM glucose indicating that these large responses are triggered by even small elevations in the concentration of glucose.
evidence: Supported by Ca2+ imaging data with fluorescent glucose tracer showing timing of responses.

claim: In isolated islets, Ca2+ responses occur with a consistent delay after the addition of glucose.
source: In contrast, in isolated islets the Ca2+ responses occurred with a consistent delay after the addition of glucose (Figure 5C, D).
evidence: Supported by Ca2+ imaging data showing delayed responses in isolated islets.

claim: The time to peak Ca2+ response is significantly shorter in slices compared to isolated islets.
source: Comparison of the parameters of the global Ca2+ responses to 16.7 mM glucose in slices with those in isolated islets (Figure 5F, G, H1) shows the time to peak mean was significantly shorter (Figure 5I) and the frequency distribution was shifted to shorter times in slices (Figure 5J).
evidence: Supported by quantification of time to peak Ca2+ response (178 ± 9 vs. 89 ± 10 s).

claim: The baseline Ca2+ signal is significantly higher in slices compared with isolated islets.
source: As before (Figure 4) we consistently observed pulsatile Ca2+ activity at 2.8 mM glucose (Figure 5A, B, E) which resulted in a significant elevation of the average 'baseline' Ca2+ signal in slices compared with isolated islets (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by quantification of baseline GCaMP6 fluorescence.

claim: Baseline Ca2+ pulses at 2.8 mM glucose are glucose dependent and lowering glucose from 2.8 to 1 mM abolishes all activity.
source: These 'baseline' Ca2+ pulses were glucose dependent and lowering glucose from 2.8 to 1 mM abolished all activity (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by Ca2+ imaging data showing loss of activity when glucose is lowered to 1 mM.

claim: β cells within slices that adjoin capillaries often show glucose-induced Ca2+ responses that originate at the capillary interface and spread rapidly across the cell.
source: (A–C) β cells within the slices that adjoin the capillaries often showed glucose (16.7 mM)-induced Ca2+ responses that originated at the capillary interface and spread rapidly across the cell (apparent velocity 50.6 ± 6.1 µm S−1, mean ± standard error of the mean [SEM], n = 7 slices from 6 animals) to the apical region.
evidence: Supported by Ca2+ imaging data showing spatiotemporal dynamics of Ca2+ waves.

claim: Ca2+ waves in slices have an apparent velocity of 50.6 ± 6.1 µm/s.
source: (A–C) β cells within the slices that adjoin the capillaries often showed glucose (16.7 mM)-induced Ca2+ responses that originated at the capillary interface and spread rapidly across the cell (apparent velocity 50.6 ± 6.1 µm S−1, mean ± standard error of the mean [SEM], n = 7 slices from 6 animals) to the apical region.
evidence: Supported by measurement of Ca2+ wave velocity from imaging data.

claim: In isolated islets, Ca2+ waves originate at the interface with capillary fragments and have a slow velocity of 1.8 ± 0.2 µm/s.
source: (D–F) In isolated islets the capillaries were fragmented, and we rarely observed Ca2+ waves. The waves we did observe originated at the interface with capillary fragments and had a slow velocity. (1.8 ± 0.2 µm S−1, mean ± SEM, n = 3 islets from 3 animals, significantly slower compared with the velocity in slices, Student's t-test p < 0.01).
evidence: Supported by measurement of Ca2+ wave velocity in isolated islets.

claim: Ca2+ wave velocity is significantly slower in isolated islets compared to slices.
source: (D–F) In isolated islets the capillaries were fragmented, and we rarely observed Ca2+ waves. The waves we did observe originated at the interface with capillary fragments and had a slow velocity. (1.8 ± 0.2 µm S−1, mean ± SEM, n = 3 islets from 3 animals, significantly slower compared with the velocity in slices, Student's t-test p < 0.01).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of Ca2+ wave velocities.

claim: During repetitive Ca2+ spiking at 2.8 mM glucose in slices, each spike shows evidence of a Ca2+ wave travelling from the capillary interface to the apical region.
source: (G) shows that during repetitive Ca2+ spiking, recorded using GCaMP6 in slices incubated in 2.8 mM glucose, each spike shows the evidence of a Ca2+ wave travelling from the capillary interface to the apical region.
evidence: Supported by Ca2+ imaging data showing spatiotemporal patterns of Ca2+ spikes.

claim: Pretreatment of slices with Y15 completely abolishes Ca2+ spikes observed at 2.8 mM glucose.
source: In our experiments, pretreatment of slices with Y15 completely abolished the Ca2+ spikes observed at 2.8 mM glucose (Figure 7A, B) and significantly reduced the responses to 16.7 mM glucose (Figure 7C, D).
evidence: Supported by GCaMP6 Ca2+ imaging data with Y15 treatment.

claim: Y15 significantly reduces Ca2+ responses to 16.7 mM glucose in slices.
source: In our experiments, pretreatment of slices with Y15 completely abolished the Ca2+ spikes observed at 2.8 mM glucose (Figure 7A, B) and significantly reduced the responses to 16.7 mM glucose (Figure 7C, D).
evidence: Supported by Fura-2 Ca2+ imaging data showing reduced peak amplitude with Y15.

claim: Y15 reduces glucose-induced insulin secretion in slices.
source: Consistent with this inhibition, Y15 reduced glucose-induced insulin secretion in slices (Figure 7E) and interestingly had no effect on high potassium-induced insulin secretion.
evidence: Supported by insulin secretion assay data with Y15 treatment.

claim: Y15 has no effect on high potassium-induced insulin secretion in slices.
source: Consistent with this inhibition, Y15 reduced glucose-induced insulin secretion in slices (Figure 7E) and interestingly had no effect on high potassium-induced insulin secretion.
evidence: Supported by insulin secretion assay data showing no difference with Y15 in high K+ condition.

claim: The cumulative number of exocytic events in response to 16.7 mM glucose over 20 min is reduced with pretreatment with Y15.
source: Using the granule fusion assay (shown in Figure 2) the cumulative number of exocytic events, in response to 16.7 mM glucose over 20 min was reduced with pretreatment with Y15 as shown when the events were mapped (Figure 7F) and quantified (Figure 7G).
evidence: Supported by quantification of granule fusion events with Y15 treatment.

claim: Targeting of granule fusion events to the capillary interface is significantly reduced in the presence of Y15.
source: Furthermore, targeting of granule fusion events to the capillary interface was significantly reduced in the presence of Y15 (Figure 7H) supporting the idea that integrin/FAK activation localises granule fusion (Gan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by quantification of fusion event targeting with Y15 treatment.

claim: Y15 fails to inhibit insulin secretion in isolated islets when stimulated with high glucose or high potassium.
source: Given our evidence that FAK activation is reduced in isolated islets (Figure 1) we tested the effect of FAK inhibition on insulin secretion in this preparation. The data show Y15 failed to inhibit insulin secretion when the islets were stimulated with high glucose or with high potassium (Figure 7I).
evidence: Supported by insulin secretion assay data in isolated islets with Y15 treatment.

claim: Integrin/FAK signaling is compromised in isolated islets.
source: This supports the idea that integrin/FAK signalling is compromised in isolated islets.
evidence: Inference based on lack of Y15 effect in isolated islets and reduced phospho-FAK.

claim: Culture of isolated β cells on laminin-coated coverslips enhances overall insulin secretion.
source: Culture of isolated β cells onto ECM-coated coverslips is known to enhance overall insulin secretion (Parnaud et al., 2006) and through local integrin activation lead to targeting of insulin granule fusion to the interface of the cells with the coverslip (Gan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Local integrin activation leads to targeting of insulin granule fusion to the interface of cells with ECM-coated coverslips.
source: Culture of isolated β cells onto ECM-coated coverslips is known to enhance overall insulin secretion (Parnaud et al., 2006) and through local integrin activation lead to targeting of insulin granule fusion to the interface of the cells with the coverslip (Gan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Cells cultured on BSA do not adhere well and grow on top of each other.
source: Cells cultured on bovine serum albumin (BSA; as an inert protein control) did not adhere well, they grew on top of each other and although phospho-FAK was apparent at the contact points of the cells with the coverslip it was sporadic and mainly on the outer edges of the cells (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images showing multilayered cell organization on BSA.

claim: Cells cultured on laminin grow as a monolayer with extensive punctate phospho-FAK staining at the footprint.
source: In contrast, cells cultured on laminin grew as a monolayer with extensive punctate phospho-FAK staining at the footprint (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images showing organized cell monolayer on laminin.

claim: Liprin and ELKS show significant enrichment at the coverslip interface when β cells are cultured on laminin.
source: Immunostaining for the synaptic scaffold proteins liprin and ELKS (Figure 8C–H) showed significant enrichment at the coverslip interface when β cells were cultured on to laminin (Figure 8D, G, H) and not on BSA (Figure 8C, E, F), which is consistent with an integrin-dependent mechanism of location both here and within slices (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification showing enrichment at laminin-cell interface.

claim: β cells cultured on laminin show large Ca2+ responses and sustained oscillations to high glucose.
source: β cells cultured on either BSA or on laminin showed glucose-induced Ca2+ responses (Figure 8I, J) but only cells on laminin showed robust long lasting Ca2+ oscillations and the overall AUC was significantly greater in the cells on laminin (Figure 8K).
evidence: Supported by Fura-2 Ca2+ imaging data comparing BSA and laminin conditions.

claim: The overall area under the curve of Ca2+ responses is significantly greater in cells cultured on laminin compared to BSA.
source: β cells cultured on either BSA or on laminin showed glucose-induced Ca2+ responses (Figure 8I, J) but only cells on laminin showed robust long lasting Ca2+ oscillations and the overall AUC was significantly greater in the cells on laminin (Figure 8K).
evidence: Supported by quantification of Ca2+ response AUC.

claim: Pretreatment with integrin-β1 function-blocking antibodies disrupts the localization of liprin at the coverslip interface.
source: In the first approach, we pretreated the cultures with integrin-β1 function-blocking antibodies (Mendrick and Kelly, 1993) and, consistent with the data in Figure 7 we saw both a disruption in the localisation of liprin at the coverslip interface and an inhibition of the glucose-induced Ca2+ responses (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing reduced liprin enrichment with integrin-β1 blocking antibody.

claim: Pretreatment with integrin-β1 function-blocking antibodies inhibits glucose-induced Ca2+ responses.
source: In the first approach, we pretreated the cultures with integrin-β1 function-blocking antibodies (Mendrick and Kelly, 1993) and, consistent with the data in Figure 7 we saw both a disruption in the localisation of liprin at the coverslip interface and an inhibition of the glucose-induced Ca2+ responses (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Ca2+ imaging data showing reduced responses with integrin-β1 blocking antibody.

claim: Y15 significantly reduces the glucose-induced Ca2+ response in β cells cultured on laminin.
source: In the second approach, we used the FAK inhibitor Y15 applied to β cells cultured on laminin-coated coverslips. In the presence of Y15, the glucose-induced Ca2+ response was significantly reduced (Figure 9A–C) and glucose-induced secretion, but not high potassium, was also inhibited in a reversible manner (Figure 9D), both consistent with the actions of Y15 in the slices (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by Fura-2 Ca2+ imaging data showing reduced AUC with Y15.

claim: Y15 reversibly inhibits glucose-induced insulin secretion but not high potassium-induced secretion in β cells cultured on laminin.
source: In the second approach, we used the FAK inhibitor Y15 applied to β cells cultured on laminin-coated coverslips. In the presence of Y15, the glucose-induced Ca2+ response was significantly reduced (Figure 9A–C) and glucose-induced secretion, but not high potassium, was also inhibited in a reversible manner (Figure 9D), both consistent with the actions of Y15 in the slices (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by insulin secretion assay data showing reversible inhibition with Y15.

claim: The distribution of liprin and ELKS is disrupted by Y15 in β cells cultured on laminin.
source: Immunofluorescence studies showed that the distribution of liprin and ELKS were disrupted by Y15 (Figure 9E–J), consistent with the data showing the importance of the integrin/FAK pathway in their positioning.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing loss of enrichment at laminin-cell interface with Y15.

claim: FAK phosphorylation is enhanced by glucose stimulation.
source: We are not the first to identify a role for FAK in the control of secretion. Halban's group showed in mouse β cells that FAK phosphorylation was increased by glucose stimulation (Rondas et al., 2011) and block of integrins or FAK inhibited insulin secretion from the MIN6 cell line with evidence that it affected F-actin remodelling (Rondas et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Block of integrins or FAK inhibits insulin secretion from the MIN6 cell line.
source: We are not the first to identify a role for FAK in the control of secretion. Halban's group showed in mouse β cells that FAK phosphorylation was increased by glucose stimulation (Rondas et al., 2011) and block of integrins or FAK inhibited insulin secretion from the MIN6 cell line with evidence that it affected F-actin remodelling (Rondas et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Knockout of FAK causes hyperglycemia in mice.
source: In a mouse study, knockout of FAK caused hyperglycemia and using isolated islets they showed a reduced insulin secretion but no effect on Ca2+ responses (Cai et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Knockout of FAK reduces insulin secretion in isolated islets but has no effect on Ca2+ responses.
source: In a mouse study, knockout of FAK caused hyperglycemia and using isolated islets they showed a reduced insulin secretion but no effect on Ca2+ responses (Cai et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: There is functional evidence for close association of Cav1.2 Ca2+ channels and insulin granule exocytosis in β cells.
source: In β cells there is functional, in vitro, evidence for close association of Cav1.2, Ca2+ channels and insulin granule exocytosis (Bokvist et al., 1995; Gandasi et al., 2017; Pertusa et al., 1999) and structural evidence for protein links between the Cav1.2 channels and syntaxin 1A (Wiser et al., 1999); a SNARE protein required for granule fusion.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Presynaptic scaffold proteins exist in β cells and function to control insulin secretion.
source: In β cells, closely analogous steps use glucose-dependent Ca2+ signals to induce insulin granule fusion, furthermore, presynaptic scaffold proteins are present (Low et al., 2014; Ohara-Imaizumi et al., 2005) and function to control insulin secretion (Fujimoto et al., 2002; Ohara-Imaizumi et al., 2005; Shibasaki et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The pancreatic slice is an important advance with closer preservation to native islet structure than isolated islets.
source: To this end, the pancreatic slice is an important advance with a closer preservation to native islet structure than isolated islets (Gan et al., 2017; Meneghel-Rozzo et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations and data showing preserved structure in slices.

claim: Endothelial cells are the only source of intra-islet ECM.
source: This is as expected, because endothelial cells are the only source of intra-islet ECM (Nikolova et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Enzymatic islet isolation results in loss of endothelial cells and capillaries.
source: A striking characteristic of islets within slices is the preservation of the rich capillary bed (Gan et al., 2017) which contrasts with the loss of endothelial cells and capillaries in the more usual method of enzymatic islet isolation (Lukinius et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations and immunostaining data showing loss of capillaries in isolated islets.

claim: The fundamental relationships between β cells and capillaries are similar between mouse and human islets.
source: We have recently shown that the fundamental relationships between β cells and capillaries are similar between mouse and human islets (Cottle et al., 2021), suggesting that the integrin/FAK pathway may play a similar role in human β cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to recent study.

claim: The integrin/FAK pathway may play a similar role in human β cells as in mouse β cells.
source: We have recently shown that the fundamental relationships between β cells and capillaries are similar between mouse and human islets (Cottle et al., 2021), suggesting that the integrin/FAK pathway may play a similar role in human β cells.
evidence: Inference based on similarity of β cell-capillary relationships between mouse and human.

claim: Both the capillary structure and ECM composition are altered in type 2 diabetes.
source: We also know that both the capillary structure (Brissova et al., 2015) and the ECM composition (Hayden et al., 2005) are altered in disease.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: β-cell function is compromised as type 2 diabetes develops, prior to loss of β-cell mass.
source: Furthermore, it is shown that β-cell function is compromised, as type 2 diabetes develops, prior to loss of β-cell mass (Cohrs et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Functional changes to β-cell responses in type 2 diabetes might result from disruption of capillaries and effects on the integrin/FAK pathway.
source: In the light of our work, it is possible that these functional changes to β-cell responses might result from disruption of the capillaries and effects on the integrin/FAK pathway we describe.
evidence: Speculation based on findings about integrin/FAK pathway and known capillary disruption in disease.

claim: Sulfonylureas can improve insulin secretion in type 2 diabetes.
source: Given that sulfonylureas can improve insulin secretion in T2D (Rorsman and Ashcroft, 2018) we already know that enhancement of glucose-dependent triggering is beneficial.
evidence: Supported by citation to established knowledge.

claim: Enhancement of glucose-dependent triggering is beneficial for type 2 diabetes treatment.
source: Given that sulfonylureas can improve insulin secretion in T2D (Rorsman and Ashcroft, 2018) we already know that enhancement of glucose-dependent triggering is beneficial.
evidence: Inference based on sulfonylurea mechanism and clinical efficacy.

claim: Stem cell-based β-cell replacement spheroids do not contain organized ECM.
source: Most approaches generate spheroids of cells that we have recently shown do not contain organised ECM (Singh et al., 2021) and, as a result, the β-like cells within the spheroids are not polarised (Singh et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent study.

claim: β-like cells within stem cell-derived spheroids are not polarized.
source: Most approaches generate spheroids of cells that we have recently shown do not contain organised ECM (Singh et al., 2021) and, as a result, the β-like cells within the spheroids are not polarised (Singh et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent study.

claim: Amplification will be the dominant pathway underpinning glucose-dependent insulin secretion in stem cell-derived spheroids.
source: Our work now suggests that amplification will be the dominant pathway underpinning glucose-dependent insulin secretion in these spheroids and that these cells will lack a drive from the integrin/FAK pathway.
evidence: Inference based on lack of ECM organization in spheroids and findings about integrin/FAK pathway.

claim: Stem cell-derived β-like cells lack a drive from the integrin/FAK pathway.
source: Our work now suggests that amplification will be the dominant pathway underpinning glucose-dependent insulin secretion in these spheroids and that these cells will lack a drive from the integrin/FAK pathway.
evidence: Inference based on lack of ECM organization and findings about integrin/FAK pathway requirement.

claim: Imposing polarity to β-like cells enhances secretion.
source: This could include imposing polarity to the β-like cells, which we have shown does enhance secretion (Singh et al., 2021), but it could also include genetic manipulation to upregulate components of the triggering pathway or the use of drugs, like sulfonylureas, to increase the sensitivity of this pathway.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.
